title: Not killing
hookLine: precept one: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life

cards: There's a spider in the bathtub. The tissue is already in your hand. And then maybe you pause, find a glass and a postcard, and walk it out to the garden like a tiny, ungrateful guest.
Why pause? It's only a spider. That pause has a place in Buddhist ethics.
After the refuges come five precepts, the basic ethics of a Buddhist life, and the first one is about exactly that moment.

teach.h: A TRAINING STEP, IN THE FIRST PERSON.
teach.b: Here it is in Pali: Panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from taking life. Look at the shape of that sentence.
It's a promise the person makes, in the first person, and the key word is sikkhapada: a training step. You're not claiming to be perfect; you're signing up to practice.
Pana means breath, or a breathing thing, so the precept reaches past people to animals, down to the spider. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line.
In Max Muller's translation: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."
That's the whole argument: everything that lives wants to go on living, just like you. Another discourse calls the five precepts great gifts.
By not killing, you give every being around you freedom from fear, and you share in that safety yourself.
Buddhists live this out in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. In Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese Buddhism, monastic custom is vegetarian.
In Theravada countries monks eat what they're given on the alms round, which can include meat, as long as they haven't seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for them.
Lay Buddhists choose differently: some are vegetarian, some aren't. Where they agree is the core: don't take a life with your own intention.
And the training starts small: the mosquito, the ant on the counter, the spider in the tub. Every one of them is a place to practice.

how: Buddhists recite the five precepts, often right after the three refuges, at temple visits and ceremonies; the first is to refrain from taking life, and some practice it by sparing insects and, in some traditions, by eating vegetarian food.

o: a chosen training to spare every breathing thing
a rule that all Buddhists must eat no meat
a strict law against harming other people

games.q: match the piece of the first precept.
p: freedom from fear for every being

s: the precepts are commandments handed down to Buddhists
each is a promise the person makes: 'I undertake the training rule.'
the first precept covers animals and insects, not only people
every Buddhist tradition requires a vegetarian diet
East Asian monastic custom is vegetarian; Theravada monks eat what they're given if it wasn't killed for them.

games.q: a mosquito lands on your arm during the evening sit. what does the first precept point toward?
o: brush it away, and let it live.
games.why: the precept covers every breathing thing, and it's a training: small moments like this are where it's practiced.

practice: Feel the breath coming in and going out: that's pana, the breath of a living thing.
Think of the smallest creature you've seen today, a fly, an ant, a bird on a wire, breathing too in its own way, wanting to go on, and rest with that for a few breaths.
Then, if you like, make a simple plan: the next insect you meet, you'll let it live, or carry it out.

wordCard.voice: Not killing. The first precept: a training, taken on freely, to refrain from taking the life of anything that breathes.

orig.note: Pali: a training rule or training step; each precept is a sikkhapada, taken on freely.

carryVoice: Your line: let it live. Every small creature wants to go on, just like you. That's day one hundred twenty-four.
